subjective.question: Explain the psychology behind a price of Rs. 9.99 instead of Rs. 10.00.
subjective.answer: Odd pricing (psychological pricing) means setting the price just below a round figure, e.g. Rs. 9.99 instead of Rs. 10.00. Psychologically, consumers read a price from left to right and register the first digits most strongly, so Rs. 9.99 is perceived as 'nine rupees something' rather than almost ten rupees. Buyers tend to ignore or round down the least significant digits instead of rounding properly, so the price feels noticeably lower than it actually is. Fractional prices also suggest to consumers that the goods are marked at the lowest possible price and that the seller has calculated the price carefully instead of charging a rough round amount. As a result, the same product appears to be a bargain, resistance to buying falls, and sales increase, although the actual difference is only one paisa.

subjective.question: Mandatory labeling is still a debatable issue in the labeling of products. What would you say in favor of mandatory labeling?
subjective.answer: Arguments in favor of mandatory labeling are: (1) Consumer protection: labels compulsorily disclose ingredients, weight, manufacturing and expiry dates, price and usage instructions, so the buyer cannot be deceived about what he is purchasing. (2) Health and safety: warnings about harmful ingredients, allergens or improper use protect consumers, especially for food, medicines and chemicals. (3) Fair competition: when every producer must declare the same information, honest firms are protected and misleading claims are reduced. (4) Informed choice: standard information allows consumers to compare competing brands on facts rather than on slogans. (5) Legal accountability: mandatory declarations fix responsibility on the manufacturer and make quality enforcement by the government possible. Therefore, despite the extra cost and packaging constraints, mandatory labeling is justified in the interest of consumers.

subjective.question: List any five characteristics of a good brand name.
subjective.answer: Five characteristics of a good brand name are: (1) It should be short, simple and easy to pronounce, spell and remember, e.g. Lux, Surf. (2) It should be distinctive and unique so that it stands out from competitors and can be legally protected and registered as a trademark. (3) It should suggest something about the product's benefits, qualities or use, e.g. 'Safeguard' suggests protection. (4) It should be adaptable and extendable to new products added to the line in the future. (5) It should not carry negative or offensive meanings in other languages and cultures where the product may be sold. In addition, a good brand name should be timeless rather than tied to a short-lived fashion, and capable of being used in advertising effectively.

subjective.question: Suppose a new detergent has been introduced in the market. List down the stages after which it will enter in the customer's buying preference list.
subjective.answer: Before a new detergent enters the customer's buying preference list, the customer passes through the stages of the adoption process: (1) Awareness: the customer first learns that the new detergent exists, usually through advertising or display, but has little information about it. (2) Interest: he becomes interested and seeks information about its features, price and benefits. (3) Evaluation: he mentally weighs the advantages and disadvantages and decides whether it is worth trying. (4) Trial: he tries the detergent on a small scale, e.g. buys a small pack or uses a free sample, to test its performance. (5) Adoption: if the trial satisfies him, he becomes a regular user of the detergent and it enters his buying preference list for repeat purchase.

subjective.question: Define marketing and explain its core concepts.
subjective.answer: Marketing is a social and managerial process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating, offering and exchanging products of value with others. Its core concepts are: (1) Needs, wants and demands: a need is a state of felt deprivation, wants are needs shaped by culture and personality, and demands are wants backed by buying power. (2) Products: anything that can be offered to a market to satisfy a need or want, including goods, services and ideas. (3) Value, cost and satisfaction: buyers choose the product that gives them the most value for their money. (4) Exchange and transactions: marketing occurs when people obtain a desired object by offering something in return. (5) Markets: a market is the set of actual and potential buyers of a product. Together these concepts form the foundation on which all marketing activities are built.

subjective.question: Differentiate between the selling concept and the marketing concept.
subjective.answer: The selling concept holds that consumers will not buy enough of the company's products unless the company undertakes a large-scale selling and promotion effort. It focuses on the needs of the seller, starts with the factory and the existing products, uses heavy selling and promotion as its means, and aims at profits through sales volume. The marketing concept, in contrast, holds that achieving organizational goals depends on determining the needs and wants of target markets and delivering the desired satisfaction more effectively and efficiently than competitors. It focuses on the needs of the buyer, starts with a well-defined target market, uses integrated marketing as its means, and aims at profits through customer satisfaction and long-term relationships. In short, selling takes an inside-out perspective while marketing takes an outside-in perspective.

subjective.question: What is Customer Experience Management? How can a company improve the customer's experience with its products and services?
subjective.answer: Customer Experience Management (CEM) is the process of strategically managing a customer's entire experience with a product and a company. Every contact a customer has with the company — before purchase, during purchase and after purchase — builds his total experience and opinion about the firm. A company can improve this experience through: (1) building an experiential platform that defines the experience it wants to deliver; (2) experiential innovation, i.e. anything that can improve the customer's own viewpoint on the firm's products and services, such as better packaging, easier usage and helpful service; (3) a friendly and responsive customer interface at every touch point; and (4) continuously engaging customers and taking their feedback. Better experiences create satisfied and loyal customers, reduce 'bad mouth' publicity and increase repeat sales and profitability.

subjective.question: Discuss the marketing environment and explain how it influences marketing decisions.
subjective.answer: The marketing environment consists of all the actors and forces outside marketing that affect management's ability to build and maintain successful relationships with target customers. It has two levels. (1) The broad (macro) environment: demographic, economic, natural, technological, political-legal and socio-cultural forces. These are largely uncontrollable and affect the whole industry; for example, inflation reduces buying power and new technology can make a product obsolete. The broad environment directly affects the task environment. (2) The task (micro) environment: the company itself, suppliers, marketing intermediaries, customers, competitors and publics, which directly influence day-to-day marketing operations. Marketing decisions must be taken after scanning both levels: the environment creates opportunities that the firm should exploit and threats against which it must defend itself through suitable strategies.

subjective.question: What is a marketing plan? List and briefly explain the main parts of a marketing plan.
subjective.answer: A marketing plan is a written document that summarizes what the marketer has learned about the marketplace and indicates how the firm plans to reach its marketing objectives; it is developed at each product, brand or product-line level and may cover one year (annual plan) or up to five years. Its main parts are: (1) Executive summary: a brief overview of the plan's goals and recommendations. (2) Current marketing situation / analysis: analysis of the market, consumers, competitors and the internal environment of the company. (3) Objectives: the financial and marketing goals of the plan in terms of sales volume, market share and profit. (4) Marketing strategy: the broad marketing approach and the positioning to achieve the objectives. (5) Action programs: what will be done, when, by whom and at what cost. (6) Financial summary: assumptions, pro-forma income statement, contribution margin and breakeven analysis. (7) Appendix: supporting research results and data.

subjective.question: Explain strategic marketing planning. Also describe the aggressiveness, innovation and market dominance strategies.
subjective.answer: Strategic marketing planning is the process of developing and maintaining a strategic fit between the organization's goals and capabilities and its changing marketing opportunities. At the corporate level the firm defines its mission, sets objectives, and decides how aggressively and innovatively it will grow. Important strategy types discussed in the course are: (1) Aggressiveness strategies, which ask whether a firm should grow and how fast: building (increasing market share and investment), holding (maintaining the present position) and harvesting (reducing investment to maximize short-term cash flow). (2) Innovation strategies, which deal with the rate of new product development: pioneers, close followers and late followers. (3) Market dominance strategies, based on market share position: market leader, market challenger, market follower and market nicher. A sound strategic plan combines these choices so that the firm uses its strengths to capture market opportunities profitably.

subjective.question: Define a product and explain its three levels with the help of an example.
subjective.answer: A product is anything that can be offered to a market that might satisfy a want or need; it is much more than a physical object — it is the complete bundle of benefits or satisfactions that buyers perceive they will obtain if they purchase it. A product has three levels: (1) Core benefit: the basic need or benefit the customer is really buying, e.g. for a car, transportation and convenience. (2) Actual product: the tangible form that delivers the core benefit — its features, design, quality level, packaging and brand name, e.g. the car's model, engine and styling. (3) Augmented product: the additional services and benefits built around the product, e.g. warranty, installation, delivery, credit availability and after-sale service and maintenance. Marketers must plan all three levels to compete effectively.

subjective.question: Explain the stages of the Product Life Cycle along with the marketing strategy appropriate for each stage.
subjective.answer: The Product Life Cycle (PLC) is the succession of stages a product goes through from its launch to its removal from the market: (1) Introduction: the product is launched, sales grow slowly and profits are negative due to heavy promotion and distribution costs; the objective is to create awareness and stimulate demand. (2) Growth: sales rise rapidly as the product becomes popular, profits improve, and most firms enter the market; the firm improves quality and adds features. (3) Maturity: sales reach their peak and then slow down; competition is intense, so firms defend market share through differentiation and price adjustments. (4) Decline: sales and profits fall because of technological advances, shifts in consumer tastes and increased competition; firms reduce promotion, cut channel members, prune weak items or withdraw from the market. The maturity and decline stages are considered defensive in nature, while introduction and growth are offensive.

subjective.question: Describe the steps involved in the New Product Development (NPD) process.
subjective.answer: The New Product Development process consists of the following steps: (1) Idea generation: systematically searching for new product ideas from customers, employees, competitors, R&D and top management; customers are the richest source of ideas. (2) Idea screening: dropping poor ideas as early as possible so that only workable ideas proceed. (3) Concept development and testing: the idea is converted into a detailed product concept and presented to target consumers to get their reactions. (4) Marketing strategy development: designing the initial marketing strategy for introducing the product. (5) Business analysis: estimating the likely selling price, sales volume, profitability and breakeven point. (6) Product development: converting the concept into a physical product or prototype. (7) Test marketing: introducing the product in a limited market to see how consumers and dealers react. (8) Commercialization: full-scale launch, deciding when, where and how to launch the product in the market.

subjective.question: Explain the consumer adoption process and the categories of adopters.
subjective.answer: The consumer adoption process is the mental process through which an individual passes from first hearing about an innovation to final adoption. Its stages are: (1) Awareness: the consumer learns the product exists but lacks information. (2) Interest: he becomes sufficiently involved to seek information about it. (3) Evaluation: he considers whether trying the product makes sense. (4) Trial: he tries it on a small scale. (5) Adoption: he decides to make full and regular use of it. On the basis of the time taken to adopt, buyers are classified into five adopter categories: Innovators (venturesome, who purchase almost as soon as the product reaches the market), Early adopters (opinion leaders with a quick response to new products), Early majority (deliberate adopters), Late majority (skeptical adopters) and Laggards (tradition-bound, last to adopt).

subjective.question: What is branding? Explain the importance of branding for sellers and buyers.
subjective.answer: A brand is a name, term, sign, symbol, design or a combination of these that identifies the goods or services of one seller or group of sellers and differentiates them from those of competitors. Branding benefits sellers in several ways: the brand name becomes the basis on which a whole story about the product's qualities can be built; it gives the seller legal protection of unique product features through trademark; it helps in segmenting markets and building a loyal customer franchise; and a strong brand creates corporate image and makes launching new products easier. For buyers, brand names help identify quality, increase shopping efficiency and assure a consistent level of satisfaction. Companies may use individual names, family branding (one brand name for several related products), company names combined with individual names, or create a fighting brand specifically to counter a competitive threat.

subjective.question: Discuss the objectives and functions of packaging and labeling.
subjective.answer: Packaging involves designing and producing the container or wrapper for a product. It has three levels: primary packaging (the material that first envelops the product and holds it, e.g. the tube of toothpaste), secondary packaging (material that provides additional protection and groups primary packages) and transport/shipping packaging (needed for storage, identification and transportation). The main objectives of packaging are: physical protection of the product, agglomeration (grouping small products together for efficiency), information transmission, convenience in handling and use, and theft reduction. Labeling is the part of packaging that carries printed information about the product — its brand, ingredients, weight, price, manufacturing and expiry dates and directions for use. Packaging and labeling together promote the product, attract attention at the point of purchase and support the brand image.

subjective.question: Define price and explain the major pricing objectives of a firm.
subjective.answer: Price is the amount of money charged for a product or service; it is the only element of the marketing mix that produces revenue, while all other elements produce costs, and it is also the most flexible element of the mix. The major pricing objectives a firm may pursue are: (1) Survival: keeping the firm alive in the short run when it faces overcapacity or intense competition. (2) Maximum current profit: setting the price that produces the maximum current profit, which requires knowledge of the demand and cost functions. (3) Maximum market share: setting the lowest possible price to win the largest market share and lower costs through volume. (4) Maximum market skimming: charging the highest initial price that customers will pay and lowering it over time. (5) Product-quality leadership: charging a premium price to signal and support superior quality. (6) Maintaining the market share and stability by meeting competitors' prices. The chosen objective guides all later pricing decisions and policies of the firm.

subjective.question: Differentiate between penetration pricing and market skimming pricing. When is each strategy suitable?
subjective.answer: Penetration pricing is the technique of setting a relatively low initial entry price for a new product, often lower than the eventual market price, in order to attract a large number of buyers quickly and win a large market share. It is suitable when the market is highly price sensitive, when production and distribution costs fall with volume (economies of scale), and when the low price discourages the entry of competitors by acting as a barrier to entry; it is commonly used for convenience goods. Market skimming pricing is the opposite strategy: the firm sets the highest initial price that the target customers will pay and then gradually lowers it. Skimming is suitable when the product is new and distinctive, buyers are less price sensitive, and the high price supports a premium image. ABC Electronics introducing a product at a high price is an example of skimming, whereas launching at a low price to capture the mass market is penetration pricing.

subjective.question: What is the marketing mix? Explain the 4Ps and their corresponding 4Cs.
subjective.answer: The marketing mix is the set of controllable marketing variables that a business combines to meet the needs of its customers and produce the desired response in the target market. It consists of the 4Ps: (1) Product: the goods or services offered, including variety, quality, design, features, brand name and packaging. (2) Price: list prices, discounts, allowances and payment periods or credit terms; it is the only element that generates revenue. (3) Place: distribution channels, coverage, locations and logistics that make the product available. (4) Promotion: advertising, sales promotion, personal selling and public relations used to communicate with customers. From the buyer's viewpoint, each P corresponds to a C: Product corresponds to Customer solution, Price to Customer cost, Place to Convenience, and Promotion to Communication. An effective marketing program blends all four elements into an integrated strategy focused on the customer.
